extracted.intended_audience: policy-makers, legal scholars, national-security practitioners, and informed public interested in surveillance and privacy
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative discussion of when and how U.S. government agencies (notably DHS/INA and FBI) may collect, analyze, retain, and share open-source social media information to prevent threats while protecting civil liberties. Covers legal constraints, operational practices, oversight, resource implications, and alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public vs. covert collection constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Government may only access publicly available social media or be overt about its identity; 'we can't lie about who we are and get into a private chat room.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationally limits agencies from covert infiltration of closed/private online spaces; shapes what methods and platforms are permissibly used for open-source collection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable belief predicate for searching
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysts 'have to look only in areas where we have a reasonable belief there's going to be information that relates to a threat'—reasonable belief is 'not a hunch, but a reasonable belief based on training, expertise.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search terms and target spaces should be chosen based on documented training and expertise; random or purely curiosity-driven monitoring is impermissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on monitoring solely for First Amendment activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are 'prohibited by the Attorney General guidelines from ... accessing any post for the purposes of just monitoring somebody's First Amendment activity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collection must be tied to a legitimate homeland/intelligence mission (e.g., threats/violence), not to surveil protected expressive or associational conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on investigative tools and authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: INA cannot use investigative tools like search warrants, Title 50/702 collection, or arrests; its role is limited to reviewing public social media and reporting ('we don't have ... we can't get search warrants. We can't do 702 surveillance. We can't ... arrest people').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different agencies have different toolkits; responsibilities and handoffs must reflect statutory limits and available authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording, reporting, and dissemination requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to record or pass along analytic findings impeded response to January 6th—analysts 'weren't recording it; to the extent that they weren't recording it, they weren't passing it along the chain.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should document collection and analysis steps, promptly share actionable intelligence with appropriate partners, and ensure internal workflows for dissemination are functional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguards about use, retention, and dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveillance activity 'needs to be surrounded by safeguards' including thinking about 'not just what they're collecting, but what they're doing with the information, how long they're retaining it, who it gets disseminated to.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should set retention limits, access controls, and dissemination rules proportionate to the intrusion and mission needs; include audits and oversight mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graduated safeguards proportional to intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be 'a graduated system ... where the safeguards are commensurate to the intrusion into speech and privacy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different collection activities (e.g., glance at trending hashtags vs. following a targeted individual, overt vs. covert engagement) require correspondingly stronger legal and procedural safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction among levels of activity (viewing vs following vs infiltration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Important legal and ethical differences exist between 'looking at social media posts generally' and 'following a particular person' or 'infiltrating a political group' (which may involve disclosure of identity, pretending to be someone else, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies must distinguish and separately authorize or prohibit each activity; higher-intrusion acts require stronger predicates and oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for oversight, checks, and legislative updating
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated references that 'institutional checks and balances ... failed' and 'Congress needs to wrestle these issues to the ground' because law and court doctrine have not kept pace with technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend congressional scrutiny, statutory updates, judicial review where appropriate, and strengthened independent oversight (IGs, Congress) to align practice with constitutional values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about guidance and training to prevent paralysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of clear guidance and leadership causes analyst paralysis (people 'back off' if they 'feel they don't have clear guidance, clear leadership, and clear support').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should issue clear, trainable rules and leadership signals so staff can act confidently within constitutional and policy bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource and organizational capacity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective open-source monitoring requires adequate staffing and capability; INA is 'tiny' (a few dozen) and not staffed like the FBI, creating structural inability to cover the mission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether to reassign responsibilities, increase staffing/training, or reconfigure roles among agencies to ensure effective mission execution consistent with constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding chilling effects and historical abuse awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveillance can chill expressive and associational activity (Civil Liberties 101); past abuses (e.g., 1950s/60s, NYPD surveillance of Muslim groups) require humility and safeguards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy design must explicitly weigh chilling effects and include affirmative protections for political speech and minority groups to avoid repeating historical harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish public social-media collection from commercial data purchases
rubrics_metrics.description: Purchasing commercially available information from data brokers can yield the same information without judicial oversight or probable cause, raising distinct legal issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different legal rules and oversight should apply to purchased commercial datasets vs. government-collected open-source material; consider judicial or statutory controls for brokered data usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to consider aggregate indicators vs individual-post analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregate trends (many posts saying 'I'm bringing my gun' or 'let's go to the Capitol') may be meaningful even if individual posts seem nonactionable ('missing the forest for the trees').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic frameworks should incorporate signal aggregation, network/contextual analysis, and methods to surface collective mobilization risks without overreaching against individuals whose single posts are ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on deputizing or outsourcing surveillance without accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Private actors can often 'do a lot more than we can in the open environment,' but becoming de facto reliance on private actors raises constitutional and oversight concerns ('we cannot make them agents of ours' but they might produce threat indicia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If government relies on private or volunteer investigators, set rules for vetting, handling of tips, evidentiary standards, and transparency to avoid quasi-governmental surveillance without safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to tailor legal framework to different collection activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Current legal doctrine 'squints at all these activities and says these look like the same thing'—there is a need for a legal framework that 'distinguishes all of these collection activities' and applies different rules to each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators and courts should map discrete collection modalities (journalistic scraping, platform-provided data, broker data, overt government collection, covert infiltration) to distinct legal regimes and protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use limited to mission-relevant threats (preventing violence/homeland threats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies assert their mission is 'collecting intelligence that's relevant to intelligence requirements' and specifically to look for social media 'that might relate to threats to the homeland' and preventing violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define mission scope narrowly in policy documents; require specificity that collection serves a homeland-protection/intelligence requirement rather than generalized monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misleading public representations of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials may misstate or overstate constraints/requirements to Congress/public; accurate description of what authorities exist matters ('their answers ... are pretty misleading').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should ensure public testimony and reporting accurately reflect operative manuals, guidelines, and legal thresholds to enable proper oversight and debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of collection value: assess effectiveness before expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: ODNI characterization that some programs had 'no intelligence value' and skepticism that failures are always about lack of information rather than failure to share/analyze.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before expanding authorities, conduct empirical evaluations of existing programs' intelligence value, information-sharing practices, and analytic capacity to use collected data effectively.
